claims.text: High-entropy alloy components can be susceptible to hot cracking during traditional fusion-welding repair.
Pulsed laser surface remelting with a pre-deposited ductile filler will produce an ultrafine repair zone.
The laser-and-filler repair will produce a metastable repair-zone microstructure.
The proposed repair will create a graded metallurgical interface between the repair zone and substrate.
The graded interface will buffer thermal stresses.
Cooling rates exceeding 10^4 K/s are a relevant processing condition for the proposed repair.
Integrated in-situ monitoring will enable precise control of filler deposition and laser-process parameters.
Rapid laser remelting minimizes the time spent in the temperature range susceptible to hot cracking.
The ductile filler layer absorbs thermal stresses.
Optimally deposited filler under monitored conditions forms a robust metallurgical bond with the substrate.
The proposed repair will improve toughness relative to conventional fusion-welding repair.
The proposed repair will reduce residual stress relative to conventional fusion-welding repair.
The proposed repair will reduce hot-crack initiation relative to conventional fusion-welding repair.
Fusion-weld solidification cracking can result from an intergranular low-melting liquid film combined with large tensile stress.
The proposed repair's performance is expected to persist under rapid thermal cycling and high mechanical loads.
The proposed repair will resist hot cracking under aggressive high-temperature and high-load service conditions.
Long-term cyclic durability across diverse service environments has not been fully validated.
The long-term stability of the filler-substrate interfacial bond and the effect of in-situ monitoring on repair uniformity require experimental validation.
